title: Sum Vectors With operator+
statement:
C++ lets a plain struct behave like a built-in numeric type for the
operators that make sense on it: define `operator+` for `Vector2D`, and
`a + b` on two `Vector2D`s becomes a normal, readable expression instead
of a named function call like `Add(a, b)`. The compiler does not know
what "add two vectors" should mean on its own -- that is exactly what the
overload supplies.

## The type

```
struct Vector2D
{
    double x;
    double y;
};
```

## Your function

Implement this exact free-function overload:

```
Vector2D operator+(const Vector2D& a, const Vector2D& b);
```

Return a new `Vector2D` whose `x` is `a.x + b.x` and whose `y` is
`a.y + b.y`. Neither `a` nor `b` is modified.

## Watch out

- **It has to be this exact free-function signature.** `operator+`
  written as a *member* function (`Vector2D Vector2D::operator+(const
  Vector2D& other) const`) also makes `a + b` compile, but it defines a
  different overload than the one this problem's harness declares and
  calls -- the harness's own declaration of the free function would then
  have nothing matching it to link against, and the build fails at the
  link step with no error pointing at a line of your code.
- **`const Vector2D&` parameters, not `Vector2D` by value.** Either
  compiles and produces the right answer, but taking a 16-byte struct by
  value copies it twice for no reason on every call -- the same
  const-reference habit that matters for a `std::vector` matters here too,
  just for a smaller object.
- **The addition is component-wise, not any other combination.** `x` adds
  to `x`, `y` adds to `y` -- there is no meaningful "cross" addition for a
  plain sum, and mixing the components up produces a value that compiles
  and looks plausible without being the vector sum at all.

tests.name: no vectors sums to the zero vector
several vectors, positive and negative components
components are not swapped or cross-added
tests.description: A sum that accidentally mixes x and y would still print two numbers -- just the wrong ones, or the right ones in the wrong slot.
